extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of classical mathematics (study of proportions, Euclid-style arithmetic)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of classical (Euclidean-style) theory of numerical proportions: definitions, continuous vs. discontinuous proportions, naming (denominations) like dupla/tripla/quadrupla, operations for composing, interpolating, multiplying denominators, and basic arithmetic manipulations of proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a proportion and denomination
rubrics_metrics.description: A proportion is the relation between quantities expressed by their denominations; names (denominationes) of proportions indicate multiplicative relations (dupla, tripla, quadrupla, etc.). A proportion between two magnitudes is named according to the multiplicative ratio of one denominator to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and verbal conventions are given: a proportion called ‘maggiore’ is that with larger denomination, ‘menore’ with smaller. The text explains that denominations may be called literally (in libraries) and that a proportion’s denomination can be changed by multiplying denominators (making it dupla, tripla, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous proportion (proportiones continuæ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of quantities is in continuous proportion when each term is to the next as the next is to the following (first:second = second:third = ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: 1,2,4,8 are continuous; the proportion from the first to the third equals the proportion from the first to the second multiplied appropriately. Rules for manipulating continuous sequences are given (multiplying denominators, identifying intermediates, forming higher-order proportionalities like dupla→quadrupla→octupla).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discontinuous (diverse) proportions and their composition
rubrics_metrics.description: When given proportions are not continuous among themselves, they may nevertheless be composed or compared by creating intermediate terms or by transforming denominations so the series can be related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how to form intermediary proportionalities (by multiplying denominators or inserting terms) to relate non-continuous proportions and to deduce resultant proportions between original extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denomination multiplication rules (forming dupla/tripla/quadrupla/etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: To change or recognize the denomination of a proportion (e.g., to make it dupla, tripla, quadrupla, octupla), multiply the denominators of the given proportions by suitable factors (powers of 2,3,4,...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: multiplying a denominator by 2 gives a dupla, by 4 a quadrupla, by 8 an octupla; repeated multiplication yields higher denominations ad infinitum. The text shows how to obtain the denominator of the composed proportion by multiplying denominators of constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for obtaining equivalent proportions by multiplying denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalent or corresponding proportions among different positions (first-to-last, first-to-third, etc.) can be produced by multiplying denominators of intermediate proportions so that the denominators align and the proportion becomes directly comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: choose multipliers so that the denominators of the intermediate ratios become equal (or fit the desired multiple), then the corresponding numerators yield the new proportion. Numerous numeric examples (1,2,4,8; sequences of .2,.4,.8 etc.) illustrate the technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation of intermediate terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two extremes, one may insert one or more intermediate terms to produce as many proportions as desired between them (creating fedecupla, decupla, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpolated terms can be placed so that the resulting chain yields any specified denomination relation; the method involves selecting terms (or multiplying denominators) to obtain the intended multiplicative step between neighbors. Examples show inserting terms so the chain contains dupla, tripla, quintupla relations among chosen positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing proportion type from denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: One recognizes whether a proportion (or an intermediate proportion) is dupla/tripla/quadrupla/etc. by examining how many times one denominator contains another (i.e., their multiplicative relationship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a denominator contains another twice it is a dupla, thrice a tripla, four times a quadrupla, etc. The text stresses checking denominators of the given intermediate terms to classify the proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding unknown extremes using known denomination
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a proportion where one extreme and the denomination relation is known, the other extreme may be found by multiplying the known extreme by the denominator (or dividing by it) as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance: to find the greater extreme from the smaller when the proportion is known as a dupla, multiply the smaller extreme by 2 (or by the appropriate multiplicative factor indicated by the denomination); conversely divide when solving the reverse problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition (sum/product) of proportions to form new proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions can be composed (added or otherwise combined) to form new proportions; the denominators of constituent proportions are used (via multiplication and summation) to determine denominators of the composite proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text indicates forming the sum/product of denominators (and possibly numerators) of component proportions to obtain the denominator of the resulting composed proportion; it gives procedural rules (e.g., multiply denominators in certain ways then sum to get new denominations) and numeric examples to demonstrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite generation of denominations by repeated multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: By repeatedly multiplying denominators (or performing the analogous operation on terms) one can produce infinitely many denominations and hence infinitely many proportional relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise emphasizes that through successive multiplications (dupla→quadrupla→octupla→… or multiplying by any integer sequence) one may form an unbounded series of proportionalities; examples show how successive powers arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportions among powers (squares, cubes, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: When dealing with squared or cubed magnitudes (quadrata, cubata), denominators multiply in higher-degree ways: to form square or cube denominational relations, multiply the denominators accordingly (squares of multipliers, cubes, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text remarks that proportions of square or cubic quantities are obtained by multiplying denominators a corresponding number of times (e.g., to get a cubic relation multiply denominators threefold), with examples sketched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equating distant terms by reducing to common denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare or determine the proportion between non-adjacent (e.g., first and last) terms in a chain, reduce intermediate ratios to common denominators by appropriate multiplications so the extreme terms can be directly compared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: multiply denominators of intermediate proportions so that the denominators aligning between the chosen extremes become equal; then deduce the proportion of the extremes. Worked numeric patterns in the text illustrate this reduction-to-common-denominator method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of proportions (continuous, discontinuous, compound/composed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportions are classified as continuous (continuæ), discontinuous/diverse (diversæ), or composed (compôse) according to whether the chain of terms forms uninterrupted equal ratios or requires composition of several proportional steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exposition explains the implications of these classifications for operations (e.g., how many intermediate terms can be inserted, when component proportions must be multiplied to relate extremes) and gives examples of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic operations on proportions: addition and subtraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides multiplication of denominators, the treatise treats the addition and subtraction of proportions (De additione proportionum ad invicem; Subtractio proportionum ab invicem) as legitimate operations with their own procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the surviving text is fragmentary, it indicates that proportions may be added or subtracted in prescribed ways and that these operations are useful and sometimes necessary; the sections are named and introduced as operational rules.
